title: The Decoy Head Trick
fact: A thorny devil carries a decoy. The knobby bump on the back of its neck works as a fake head. When threatened, the lizard tucks its real head down between its front legs, leaving the decoy on show while the real one stays protected.
quote: These small lizards grow to 8 inches (20 centimeters) long and have evolved an impressive set of defenses, including an appendage on the back of the necks that acts as a "'false head." When threatened, the lizards tuck their real head down between their front legs, leaving the fake head exposed while protecting the real head.
note: Live Science profile, 2024-08-31. Parks Australia (uluru.gov.au) separately calls it 'a knob-like false head on its shoulders'.

title: 750 Ants a Day
fact: Thorny devils eat nothing but ants. A devil settles beside an ant trail and picks them off as they march past. Ants are not very nourishing, so it takes an estimated 750 a day. Feeding averages 2.9 ants a minute, and devils have been clocked at up to one ant per second.
publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology
quote: Thorny devils are obligate myrmecophages; they eat only ants. ... They are "sit-and-wait" predators, finding a feeding site near cover and waiting for their ant prey to pass. Iridomyrmex species are eaten as they pass in terrestrial trails ... Because ants contain chitin and formic acid and are relatively low in nutritive value, large amounts must be consumed. Thorny devils have large stomachs to accommodate consuming large numbers of ant prey; it is estimated that they eat 750 ants daily. Feeding rates averaged 2.9 ants per minute, but rates up to 1 ant per second were recorded.
note: Other sources give other figures (Parks Australia: 'thousands of ants in a day'); the card uses ADW's only.

title: Blurry on Purpose
fact: Glass frogs are always green, but they look brighter or darker to match the leaf they sit on. Their legs are more see-through than their bodies, so with the legs tucked in at rest, the frog's outline fades gradually into the leaf instead of making a sharp edge. Scientists call this edge diffusion.
quote: the study published in PNAS reveals that, while glass frog translucency does act as camouflage, the mechanism differs from that of true transparency. ... “The frogs are always green but appear to brighten and darken depending on the background. This change in brightness makes the frogs a closer match to their immediate surroundings, which are predominantly made up of green leaves. We also found that the legs are more translucent than the body and so when the legs are held tucked to the frog’s sides at rest, this creates a diffuse gradient from leaf colour to frog colour rather than a more salient sharp edge. This suggests a novel form of camouflage: ‘edge diffusion’.”
note: Press release 2020-05-25 on Barnett et al., PNAS 2020; quote is lead author James Barnett.

title: Night Shift Parents
fact: Glass frog eggs hang on leaves over streams, a tasty snack for snakes and insects. A study of at least 40 species found parental care in every one sampled. In many species the mother broods the eggs on their first night. In almost a third, the father stands guard far longer, even after the eggs start hatching.
quote: Glassfrog eggs, laid on leaves hanging over streams in tropical rainforests, are tasty snacks for snakes, insects, and other predators until they hatch and drop into the streams to begin life as tadpoles. ... Delia ... went on to observe nighttime parental behavior among no fewer than 40 species of glassfrogs ... in many species, glassfrog mothers brood their eggs during the night the eggs are fertilized, and that this care improves the survival of the eggs, while in almost a third of species, glassfrog fathers stay on guard for much longer periods. ... found, to the scientists’ surprise, parental care in every glassfrog species that they sampled. ... “Even after eggs have started hatching, fathers keep caring.”
note: BU Today on Delia et al., Journal of Evolutionary Biology 2017. The old candidate ('in many glass frogs the males guard the eggs') was inaccurate: mothers brood in many species, fathers guard longer in almost a third.

title: Last Stand in the Canals
fact: Wild axolotls live in just one place on Earth: the canals and wetlands of Xochimilco in Mexico City. Surveys counted an estimated 6,000 per square kilometer in 1998 and just 36 in 2014, a 99 percent drop. A newer survey netted none at all, though DNA traces in the water show some still survive.
quote: These wetlands, cradled within North America’s most populous city, are the only place on Earth where you can find one of the most recognizable — and endangered — creatures on the planet: the axolotl. ... Although no axolotls were captured with the nets, eDNA testing, which captures traces of animals’ genetic material in water, soil or even air, revealed that axolotls are still present in the canals. ... In 1998, there were an estimated 6,000 axolotls per square kilometer. By 2014, the last time the survey was conducted, that number had dwindled to just 36 per square kilometer — a 99 percent decrease.
note: Article dated 2025-08-12. A second census phase was planned for September 2025; recheck for newer numbers on the day it ships.

title: A Nest Built for One
fact: A shoebill can lay one to three eggs, five days apart, but usually only one chick survives to fly. The reason is grim: the older chick kills the younger one. It is called siblicide, and it has been caught on film in Zambia's Bangweulu Wetlands.
publisher: NatureUganda and ZSL EDGE of Existence
quote: They are able to lay 1-3 eggs, at an interval of 5 days with one chick usually fledging to maturity due to siblicide, where the older chick kills the younger one (Dodman, 2013). This siblicide was illustrated by the video footage of taken from Bangweulu Wetlands in Zambia (BBC 2013).
note: Shoebill Survival Blueprint (2018), section 1.4. National Geographic separately: 'Only one chick typically survives to fledge.'

title: Cooling Off by the Billful
fact: Both shoebill parents tend the eggs: they incubate them, turn them and even cool them down, using water they carry to the nest in their huge bills. It works like a built-in bucket for nest-side air conditioning. The eggs hatch in about a month.
quote: As co-parents, both birds tend to the eggs and young. This includes incubating and turning eggs, and cooling them with water they bring to the nest in their large bills. Hatching occurs in about a month.
note: Same page confirms a spare: 'Shoebills are in a family all their own, though they were once classified as storks' and their closest relatives are the pelicans.

title: The Penguin Wave
fact: Emperor penguins in a winter huddle are packed so tightly that no bird can move on its own. So every 30 to 60 seconds, they all take small steps together, and the movement travels through the huddle like a wave. Over time these shuffles reorganize the whole huddle, giving each penguin a chance at time inside it.
quote: Penguins in a huddle are packed so tightly that individual movements become impossible ... It is crucial, however, that the huddle structure is continuously reorganized to give each penguin a chance to spend sufficient time inside the huddle, compared with time spent on the periphery. Here we show that Emperor penguins move collectively in a highly coordinated manner to ensure mobility while at the same time keeping the huddle packed. Every 30–60 seconds, all penguins make small steps that travel as a wave through the entire huddle. Over time, these small movements lead to large-scale reorganization of the huddle.
note: Zitterbart, Wienecke, Butler and Fabry 2011. Animal is 'Penguin' to match the Beastfile's factAnimal. The old fun fact's 'no one stays on the cold edge for long' is stronger than the paper.

title: Counting Crows
fact: Carrion crows can plan how many calls to make. In a lab study, three crows saw a numeral or heard a cue sound, then called one to four times to match it and pecked an enter key when done. All three succeeded, and the sound of the first call even predicted how many would follow.
quote: Crows can deliberately plan how many calls to make ... Together with his team he undertook behavioral experiments with three carrion crows ... on seeing a selection of Arabic numerals or on hearing specific sounds they had to produce one to four calls as appropriate and then conclude their call sequence by pecking on an enter key. All three birds succeeded in this. ... Using the acoustic properties of the first call in a numerical sequence we could predict how many calls the crow would make
note: Press release 2024-05-23 for Liao, Brecht, Veit and Nieder, Science 2024, doi 10.1126/science.adl0984.
